title: Sampling distributions of estimators
dek: An estimator is a function of the data. Its sampling distribution is the law of that function under repeated draws from the model — not the histogram of yesterday’s point estimates.
story: θ̂ = T(Y₁,…,Yₙ) is a random variable because the data are. A sampling distribution is the law of T under the model you claimed. A standard error is an estimated standard deviation of that law. A confidence interval is a set-valued function of the data with a coverage claim under that same law.

You do not get to see the sampling distribution from one experiment. You approximate it with asymptotics (Normal, χ²), with a bootstrap, or with simulation from a fitted model. Mixing those three without naming which one you used is how methods sections become folklore.

Bias, variance, and MSE are properties of the sampling distribution. “This estimate is biased” said about a single number is a category error unless you mean “this procedure is biased.” In a TB survey with n = 12 districts, the procedure’s bias can dwarf the pretty SE printed by software.
deep: If θ̂ is approximately N(θ, v/n), then se = √v̂/n is a plug-in. Coverage of θ̂ ± 1.96 se is a statement about the procedure, P(interval covers θ) → 1−α, not about the posterior probability that θ sits in today’s interval.

Monte Carlo check: draw Y^(b) from f(·|θ₀), compute T^(b), look at the histogram. If your analytic SE does not match sd(T^(b)), believe the simulation for that finite n and go find the regularity you broke (boundary, sparse events, dependence).

The bootstrap (next plate) resamples the empirical distribution instead of the parametric f. Parametric bootstrap resamples f(·|θ̂). They answer related but not identical questions, especially under model misspecification.

In WGS–DST, the sampling unit is usually the isolate, not the SNP. A sampling distribution that pretends 400,000 sites are iid observations of one scientific parameter is a fiction; the relevant n is closer to the number of independent lineages.

formulas.label: Standard error
formulas.note: An estimate of the sampling SD, not the SD of the scientific error of one number in a moral sense.

formulas.label: Mean squared error
formulas.note: Bias–variance lives here. Consistency is MSE → 0, not “unbiased for finite n.”

visual.caption: Three cartoon sampling laws for the same estimator: a well-behaved large-n Normal, a small-n skew (events are rare), and a tighter law after you actually increased n. The x-axis is the estimator, not the raw observation.

example.title: SE of a resistance proportion
example.setup: n = 25 isolates, y = 5 with a high-confidence katG S315T. Estimator π̂ = y/n. Model: iid Bernoulli(π). What sampling law are you quoting with se = √(π̂(1−π̂)/n)?

steps.title: Exact law
steps.body: nπ̂ ~ Binomial(n, π). That is the sampling distribution. It is discrete and, at π = 0.1, still noticeably skewed.

steps.title: Normal approximation
steps.body: se ≈ √(0.2×0.8/25) = √0.0064 = 0.08. A Wald interval 0.20 ± 1.57×0.08 is using a Normal stand-in for the binomial law. With 5 events, a score interval is the less theatrical object.

steps.title: Monte Carlo check
steps.body: Simulate Binomial(25, 0.2) a few thousand times. If the histogram’s SD is ~0.08, the formula matched the model. If isolates are household-clustered, the simulated SD from a hierarchical draw will exceed 0.08 — that is the missing covariance.

example.takeaway: Name the law of the estimator. The printed SE is only as honest as that law.

choices: The probability that θ̂ equals θ
An estimate of the standard deviation of the estimator under the sampling model
The posterior SD of θ by definition
check.answer: An estimate of the standard deviation of the estimator under the sampling model
check.why: SE is a sampling-distribution object. A posterior SD is a different number with a different meaning.

whyWrong.The probability that θ̂ equals θ: That is usually zero in continuous models.
whyWrong.The posterior SD of θ by definition: Only if you are doing Bayes and even then you should not rename it SE without comment.
whyWrong.The residual of a GLM: Residuals are on observations, not on the estimator’s law.

check.prompt: iid Bernoulli, n = 100, π̂ = 0.09. Model-based se(π̂) is closest to:

whyWrong.0.09: That is π̂, not its SE.
whyWrong.0.9: Off by a factor of n.
whyWrong.0.003: That is roughly the variance 0.000819, not the SD.

check.prompt: On the sampling-distribution plate, the x-axis is the estimator. What would be a misreading?
check.figureHint: Three curves labelled as laws of θ̂.
choices: Treating those curves as the sampling model of a single observation Yᵢ
Noticing that bigger n tightens the law of θ̂
Using the plate to remember that θ̂ is random
check.answer: Treating those curves as the sampling model of a single observation Yᵢ
check.why: The plate is about T(Y), not about Yᵢ. Conflating them is the classic “histogram of the data versus histogram of the estimator” error.

whyWrong.Noticing that bigger n tightens the law: That is the point of the third curve.
